meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: The organising fact on this board is no longer any single central bank: it is the long end of the US curve. The ten-year Treasury yield touched 5.342% on October 1, its highest since early 2002, after rising 87.1bp across the third quarter - the sharpest quarterly increase since 1994 - and the ten-year TIPS real yield sits at 2.88%. That single number explains most of what looks contradictory elsewhere: gold is down 6.45% on the month and silver 8.57% in the middle of an active Gulf war, equities in Europe hit three-and-a-half-month lows, and the dollar printed a yearly high at 101.935 on DXY even though Tuesday's core PCE came in soft at 3.0% y/y against 3.3% expected. Havens are losing to real rates, and that applies to the franc exactly as it applies to bullion. The second regime fact is that yesterday's energy relief has fully reversed: Brent is 102.018 and up 4.70% on the week, WTI 92.430 after settling 2.7% higher at 92.87, and the Hormuz blockade restarted on July 14 still chokes roughly 20% of global daily energy throughput. That is what has every central bank except the BoC and SNB hiking into weakening labour markets.
meta.nextBigEvent: US payrolls today at 12:30Z: 89K forecast against 162K prior, unemployment 4.1%, average hourly earnings 0.3% m/m. With the October 28 hike a minority call and December near 90% cumulative, this print decides whether the front end re-converges with the long end. The euro area September flash HICP lands three and a half hours earlier at 09:00Z, forecast 3.7% from 3.3%.

dailyRead: Read today through the long end of the US curve, because almost every cross-asset oddity on this board resolves there. The ten-year Treasury yield touched 5.342% on October 1, the highest since early 2002, capping a third quarter in which it rose 87.1 basis points - the sharpest quarterly move since 1994 - before easing back toward 5.27%. The ten-year TIPS real yield is 2.88%. Hold that number in mind and the contradictions dissolve: gold is 4185.22 and down 6.45% on the month, silver 61.222 and down 8.57%, both falling hard in the middle of an active Gulf war that has Brent above 100 dollars. The haven bid is not absent; it is being outbid by real rates. The same logic is why the franc is the weakest currency here at -2 and why the dollar printed a yearly high of 101.935 on DXY despite a genuinely soft core PCE on Tuesday at 3.0% y/y against 3.3% expected. The front end was repriced dovish last week and the dollar rose anyway, because what is driving it is the long end, persistent inflation and the supply of government paper, not the October meeting. The single new fact that moves this board today is Japanese. Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7% y/y for September against a 2.4% forecast and 1.8% prior, the fastest in ten months, and the core-core measure the BoJ actually watches for trend inflation rose to 3.0% from 2.0%. That matters because yesterday I cut JPY from +2 to +1 on a specific fact - the BoJ's own Summary of Opinions from the September meeting damped expectations of a back-to-back October hike - and this print is the direct answer to it, landing four weeks before an October 29-30 meeting that publishes a fresh quarterly Outlook Report with new inflation forecasts. That leg of yesterday's thesis has broken, so JPY goes back to +2 and the yen is among today's firmer majors with USD/JPY at 157.850 from 158.279. Be honest about the tension in that call: the yen still faces the worst carry on the board against a 5.3% ten-year, which is why USD/JPY is RANGE rather than SHORT and why I would rather express a firm yen against the franc, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar than against the dollar. CHF/JPY at 190.220 is the widest score gap here at four points and the cleanest single ticket on the page: zero policy rate against a central bank at a thirty-year high, and the SNB has just stopped threatening to defend the franc. On September 24 it held at zero and quietly returned to its standard wording on FX intervention, dialling down the war footing because the franc had already weakened about 3% trade-weighted since June, while nudging its inflation forecasts up to 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for 2027 and 2028. A funding currency whose central bank no longer wants it stronger, in a world of 5.3% yields, is a short against almost anything. The day is front-loaded with two releases and the order matters. At 09:00Z the euro area September flash HICP is forecast at 3.7% from 3.3%, with core at 2.5%. The ECB hiked its deposit rate to 2.50% on September 10 and said the Middle East conflict continues to generate inflation pressure with inflation set to remain well above target for an extended period, but October 29 has drifted toward a pause after three Lagarde appearances this week struck a more measured tone. I keep EUR at +1 and genuinely two-sided: a 3.7% or higher print puts that meeting back in play, and note that the gas retracement the pause case rests on is not really happening - EU gas is 73.47 and up 2.20% on the week, German gas 74.98 and up 1.90% on the day, both still up around 150% on the year. Then at 12:30Z US payrolls, forecast 89K against 162K prior with unemployment 4.1% and earnings 0.3%. The forecast sits exactly at the level the September SEP carries for unemployment across its whole horizon, so a print at or below 89K with soft earnings makes even December a question, while a beat puts October 28 back in play inside a day. Sterling is the quiet hawkish story and deserves more respect than its score implies. The BoE held at 3.75% on September 17 but the vote was 6-3, with Pill, Mann and Greene all voting for 4.00%, and the Bank expects inflation around 3.75% in Q4 and slightly above 4% in early 2027. Bailey spoke again on October 1 and made the conditional explicit: higher global energy costs have so far had limited effect on UK price and wage setting, but the longer the volatility persists the more likely it is the Bank will need to raise Bank Rate. With UK gas at 186.53 GBp/thm and up 152.72% on the year, that condition is being met rather than relieved, and GBP/USD at 1.32096 has held up better on the month at -2.34% than any European peer. November 5 is the meeting. The antipodeans split on policy rather than on risk, which makes AUD/NZD the cleanest expression of either. The RBA hiked to 4.60% on September 29 - its fourth of 2026, unanimous 9-0, a fifteen-year high - with Bullock saying more hikes are not off the table while hoping four will prove restrictive enough; markets price roughly one-in-three for November 3. The RBNZ by contrast raised to 2.75% on September 2 and published a track pointing to a pause in October and a hike in December, and even at 3.00% the OCR would sit three-quarters of a point below the floor of the Fed's range, so the kiwi's rate gap stays negative whatever happens on October 28. NZD/USD at 0.56126 is the worst major of the month at -4.55% and the lowest since the RBNZ's last cut in November 2025. I am holding AUD at 0 rather than promoting it, because nothing new arrived today: the highest policy rate on this board and a copper squeeze still sit against an unemployment rate that has climbed to 4.6% and a pair that cannot reclaim 0.70. Copper is the one metal that has decoupled and the leg that would resolve AUD upward - 6.5255 a pound, up 0.67% on the day and 14.85% on the year, powered by Chinese physical buying and thin exchange inventories against a refined deficit JP Morgan puts near 330,000 tonnes for 2026, while gold and silver lose to the real-rate shock. Canada keeps the widest clean policy gap to the dollar at 175 basis points after a seventh consecutive hold at 2.25%, with August employment at -41.7K and full-time down 35.9K, so CAD stays at -1. But the oil leg of that thesis has flipped since yesterday and I will not pretend otherwise: Brent back above 100 is a direct terms-of-trade tailwind, which is why USD/CAD at 1.42159 is only a MEDIUM long and why I prefer CAD long against the franc and the kiwi to CAD short against the dollar. European equities are the clearest read-through from the bond shock, and the EU50 leg worth naming is that banks led Thursday's decline by more than 3.5% even as the curve rose - the discount-rate shock is beating the margin story that usually makes a steeper curve good for the index's heaviest sector, with French and Italian political risk still underneath. The DAX fell about 1% to 24,939 on Thursday, its lowest since July 23, on exactly the two things that are not reversing: rising oil and elevated yields.

USD.when: December 9 remains the live meeting rather than October 28, but today's payrolls at 12:30Z can move that inside a day. Prediction markets put the October 28 hike in the minority - around 28% on one read with roughly 73% for a hold, against a 65% hike print on another venue, so treat the exact number as unsettled rather than precise. Cumulative pricing through December 9 is the stable part at roughly 90% for at least one more 25bp move
USD.note: TE re-verified: the upper bound of the fed funds target range is 4.00%, raised from 3.75% on September 16 in a unanimous decision - the first increase since 2023. The September SEP median is 4.1% for year-end with the second-year projection at 3.9%, both revised up sharply from 3.6% and 3.4%, PCE inflation projected at 3.7% for 2026 with core at 3.4%, GDP at 2.3% and unemployment at 4.1% across the horizon; Chair Warsh again declined to submit his forecasts. What has not changed in a week of dovish front-end repricing is the direction, which is why this stays on hike. Tuesday's core PCE printed 0.2% m/m against 0.3% forecast with the y/y at 3.0% against 3.3% expected and headline at 3.4% against 3.7% - genuinely soft, and below the Committee's own 3.4% core projection - yet the dollar made a yearly high anyway, because the long end is being driven by persistent inflation, heavy issuance and strong growth rather than by the next meeting. Final GDP was revised up to 2.2% annualised from 1.5% and ADP came in at 90K against 73K. John Williams supplied the dovish words, pushing back on an imminent follow-up and saying there is no urgency while still seeing one more hike as potentially appropriate this year; Goolsbee called inflation above target for five and a half years playing with fire, and Barkin indicated more hikes are likely needed. Waller spoke on October 1 but at a data conference on FRED and AI, offering no policy or outlook comment at all - a non-event by design that closed a repricing channel rather than opening one. The hawkish data point of the week was ISM manufacturing prices at 77.9 against 72.3 expected and 71.1 prior. Today's payrolls forecast of 89K from 162K, with unemployment at 4.1% and earnings at 0.3%, sits exactly at the SEP's unemployment path: at or below forecast with soft earnings makes December a real question, a beat puts October back in play. The FY2027 continuing resolution is signed through December 11, so there is no shutdown risk to the release. FOMC minutes from September follow on October 7.

EUR.when: December is now the base case rather than October 29, though today's 09:00Z flash HICP can restore the October meeting. Goldman Sachs Research expects the next 25bp move in December, taking the deposit rate to 2.75%
EUR.note: TE re-verified: the ECB deposit facility rate is 2.50%, raised from 2.25% on September 10 - note TE's headline euro-area Interest Rate row shows 2.65%, which is the main refinancing rate, not the policy rate this board uses. The September statement said the conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures and that inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period, and the Bank raised both its inflation and its growth forecasts. Since then the tone has softened: Lagarde appeared three times between September 28 and October 1 and struck a more measured note, which together with an assumed retracement in gas prices has moved the bar for an October 29 hike higher. October is still described as live, but the balance of risks has shifted toward a pause absent a renewed leg higher in energy. The honest caveat is that the gas retracement underpinning that view is not visible in the prints: EU gas is 73.47 EUR/MWh and up 2.20% on the week, German gas 74.98 and up 1.90% on the day, and both remain up around 150% on the year. Today at 09:00Z the September flash HICP is forecast at 3.7% y/y from 3.3%, with core flash at 2.5% from 2.4%; TE still carries August headline at 3.2%, revised down from a 3.3% preliminary. A print at or above forecast puts October 29 back into contention and is the single thing most likely to move EUR crosses today. The decision is at 13:15Z with the press conference at 13:45Z.

GBP.when: November 5 is the live meeting and the vote is already close. Three of nine members voted to hike in September, so two converts would do it, and Bailey has made the trigger explicit and conditional on energy persistence
GBP.note: TE re-verified: Bank Rate is 3.75%, held on September 17. The vote is the story - 6-3, with Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene all voting for an immediate increase to 4.00%, and no member voting for a cut. The Bank expects inflation to rise further, to around 3.75% in Q4 2026 and slightly above 4% in early 2027 on mid-September energy prices, against an August CPI of 3.1% and core at 2.6%. Bailey's formulation at the decision and again in his October 1 remarks is the thing to trade: higher global energy costs have so far had a limited effect on UK price and wage setting, but the longer the volatility persists the bigger the impact on inflation and the more likely it is that Bank Rate will need to rise to return inflation to 2%. That condition is being met rather than relieved - UK gas is 186.53 GBp/thm, up 1.88% on the day and 152.72% on the year. Against the hawkish case, the labour side is cooling: July employment change slowed to +67K from +83K, wage growth eased to 3.9% from 4.2%, vacancies fell to 702K and the unemployment rate is 4.9%. Growth was revised up to 1.4% y/y. The combination of a 6-3 split, an explicit energy trigger and a soft labour market is why GBP sits at +1 with a hawkish forward rather than higher.

JPY.when: October 29-30 is live again after this morning's Tokyo CPI, and it is the meeting that publishes a fresh quarterly Outlook Report with new inflation forecasts - the natural vehicle for a hike the Bank wants to justify
JPY.note: TE re-verified: the BoJ policy rate is 1.25%, raised from 1.00% on September 18 and the highest since 1995. The reason this entry changes today is a single print. Tokyo core CPI for September, released at 23:30Z on October 1, rose 2.7% y/y against a 2.4% median forecast and 1.8% in August - the fastest in ten months - while the index stripping fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches as its better gauge of trend inflation, rose 3.0% from 2.0%. A beat across the measures lifts pricing for an October move and pushes short-dated JGB yields up. That directly answers the fact I cut JPY on yesterday: the BoJ's own Summary of Opinions from the September meeting had damped expectations of a back-to-back October hike, and this data undercuts that damping four weeks before the decision. National CPI remains 1.9% with core at 1.7%, so Tokyo is the leading edge rather than the confirmation. Supporting the hawkish case: wage growth at 4.7% in July from 4.0%, unemployment at 2.5%, bank lending up 5.4% y/y, and a monetary base contracting 15.2% y/y as the Bank runs down its balance sheet. Against it: the yen still carries the worst funding disadvantage on this board against a 5.3% US ten-year, and a weak yen is itself part of why the BoJ is tightening. The decision and the Outlook Report both land at 03:00Z on October 30, with the Summary of Opinions from that meeting on November 9.

AUD.when: November 3 at 03:30Z, but it is a minority call: markets price roughly one-in-three for a fifth hike, and Bullock has said she hopes four will prove restrictive enough
AUD.note: TE re-verified: the RBA cash rate is 4.60%, raised from 4.35% on September 29 - the fourth hike of 2026, delivered unanimously by all nine Board members, and a fifteen-year high. It is the highest policy rate on this board. The statement said higher rates are needed to slow the economy and return inflation to target, that inflation remains elevated with some of the upside risks flagged in August now materialising, and that the Board will do what it considers necessary including increasing the cash rate further if needed. Bullock noted inflation has been outside the target band for six years. The August monthly CPI released on September 30 was 4.0% y/y against a 4.1% forecast and 3.5% prior - an acceleration that just missed consensus - with the trimmed mean at 3.6%. The two-sided part is the real economy: unemployment has climbed to 4.6% from 4.5%, GDP growth slowed to 2.1% y/y from 2.5%, and wage growth is stable at 3.2%, well below headline inflation. August employment did rebound +39.5K after -15.9K, but full-time work fell 6,282. Private sector credit is running at 8.4% y/y. The external support is copper at 6.5255 USD/lb, up 14.85% on the year on a physical squeeze, which is the leg that would resolve AUD upward. Meeting minutes land October 13.

NZD.when: October 28 at 01:00Z should be a pause on the Bank's own published track, with the next hike pencilled for December 9. Market pricing is genuinely split - one read has about 88% for no change, another about 80% for a hike to 3.00% - so the bank's own track is the more reliable anchor here
NZD.note: TE re-verified: the RBNZ official cash rate is 2.75%, raised from 2.50% on September 2. The rate track the Bank published alongside that decision points to a pause in October and a further increase in December, which is why this entry reads hold rather than hike despite the tightening direction. The arithmetic that matters for the currency is unchanged either way: even at 3.00% the OCR would sit three-quarters of a point below the floor of the Fed's 3.75-4.00% range, so the kiwi's rate gap to the dollar stays negative whatever happens on October 28. The data is a stagflationary mix - Q2 CPI jumped to 4.1% from 3.1%, core to 3.2%, while the unemployment rate rose to 5.6% from 5.4% and quarterly GDP growth slowed sharply to 0.2% from 0.9% even as the annual rate improved to 2.6%. Wage growth is 2.1%, the weakest on this board. NZD/USD at 0.56126 is the worst major of the month at -4.55% and the lowest since the RBNZ's final cut of the prior easing cycle in November 2025, and it kept sliding this week as US yields outweighed stronger Chinese data. A Financial Stability Report follows on November 10 and the next decision on December 9.

CAD.when: October 28 at 13:45Z, alongside a Monetary Policy Report, and an eighth consecutive hold is the clear base case. Oil above 100 dollars and a labour market shedding jobs are pulling the Bank in opposite directions, which is itself an argument for staying still
CAD.note: TE re-verified: the BoC overnight rate is 2.25%, held on September 2 for the seventh consecutive meeting and unchanged since the easing cycle ended. It is the lowest policy rate on this board bar the SNB's zero, leaving a 175bp gap to the upper bound of the Fed's range - the widest clean policy gap here. The labour market is the weak leg and it is genuinely weak: August employment fell 41.7K after +75.1K, full-time work dropped 35.9K, and average monthly job growth across 2026 is effectively zero at about -5K, with the unemployment rate at 6.4% and wage growth decelerating to 3.2% from 3.4%. The Bank's own projection has GDP growth at 1.1% for 2026 and 1.5% for 2027, enough to gradually absorb the excess supply created by US trade restrictions, with excess supply roughly offsetting upward cost pressures to keep inflation near 2%. Headline CPI is 3.0% with core at 2.4%, and Q2 GDP came in at 1.1% y/y from 0.1%. What has changed since yesterday is the offset: Brent is back above 100 dollars and up 4.70% on the week, and for a major crude exporter that is a direct terms-of-trade tailwind. It does not change the policy path but it does cap USD/CAD, which is why the long there is MEDIUM rather than HIGH. A Business Outlook Survey and Survey of Consumer Expectations land October 19.

CHF.when: December 10 at 08:30Z is the next assessment and a hold at zero is overwhelmingly likely. The interesting question is no longer the rate but the intervention stance, and that has just moved in the franc-negative direction
CHF.note: TE re-verified: the SNB policy rate is 0.00%, held on September 24 and the lowest in the world. The decision mattered for the FX stance rather than the rate. The Bank dialled down its threat of currency intervention, returning to its standard wording that it is willing to be active in the foreign exchange market as necessary, after the franc had already depreciated about 3% on a trade-weighted basis since the June assessment - effectively ending the war footing it had adopted over franc strength, and pivoting toward more vigilance on inflation. It raised its conditional inflation projections slightly across the horizon, to average annual rates of 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for both 2027 and 2028, noting inflation has risen since June primarily on higher energy prices, and put 2026 GDP growth at 1.5-2%. TE's September CPI confirms the direction at 1.0% y/y from 0.8%, with core at 0.5% from 0.4% - rising, but from a base so low that it buys the franc nothing in carry terms. The Bank sold CHF1.4bn in the second quarter as the Iran war stoked safe-haven demand. The structural point for this board is simple: a zero-rate currency whose central bank has stopped wanting it stronger, in a world where the US ten-year yields 5.3% and real yields are 2.88%, is the natural funding leg. Minutes from the September assessment are published October 22.

Invalidated by payrolls at or below 89K with earnings soft, which would drag December into question and finally let the long end rally - the one scenario that reverses the dollar, gold and the franc all at once.

Dialling down the intervention threat removes the force that used to cap franc weakness, and it did so explicitly because the franc had already fallen 3% trade-weighted - a central bank content with a weaker currency, at zero, is the natural short. The deeper point is that the haven bid has failed here for the same reason it has failed in gold: real rates at 2.88% outbid it, on escalation days and de-escalation days alike. Invalidated by a disorderly Hormuz escalation large enough to make havens trade on fear rather than on carry, or by US payrolls weak enough to collapse real yields.

catalysts.note: The ten-year at 5.342% on October 1 was the highest since early 2002 after +87.1bp in Q3, the sharpest quarterly rise since 1994, with the TIPS real yield at 2.88%. This is the variable that is currently setting the dollar, gold, the franc and European equities simultaneously - watch it ahead of any single central bank.

geopolitics: The Iran war remains the inflation engine underneath every rate path on this board, and this week it stopped being a disinflationary story. The Strait of Hormuz blockade, restarted on July 14 after the April ceasefire and June memorandum broke down, still chokes roughly 20% of global daily energy throughput. Brent is 102.018 and up 4.70% on the week, WTI 92.430 after settling 2.7% higher at 92.87, gasoline up 5.48% on the week, and the year-to-date numbers show the structural damage rather than the noise: Brent +67.65%, WTI +60.97%, EU gas +160.90%, UK gas +152.72%, German gas +149.92%. War-risk insurance for the passage is priced at many multiples of pre-crisis levels and several protection and indemnity clubs have withdrawn cover outright, so the constraint is shipping capacity and insurability rather than reserves. Gulf producers have had to curtail output as storage hit capacity and alternative export routes remain insufficient. The diplomacy is close but conditional: Iran and Oman have agreed a transit route and are finishing arrangements for jointly managing the waterway, yet any reopening depends on the United States ending its own naval blockade of Iranian ports, and efforts to resolve the broader conflict were reported stalled this week. S&P Global no longer assumes a definitive end to the war or a return to normal in the strait by the end of 2027, and expects oil to hold an 80-100 dollar range through next year. The FX transmission runs in three directions and they do not all point the same way. First, into inflation and therefore into policy: this is why the ECB warned the conflict continues to generate inflation pressure with inflation well above target for an extended period, why Bailey has tied a November BoE hike explicitly to how long energy volatility persists, why the SNB raised its projections while holding at zero, and why Australia, New Zealand and Japan are all tightening into softening labour markets. It is a supply shock being met with demand restraint across eight economies at once. Second, into terms of trade, which is the leg that changed since yesterday: Canada is the one major crude exporter here and Brent above 100 is a direct tailwind, enough to cap USD/CAD even though the BoC will hold an eighth time and the labour market is shedding jobs. Third, and most counter-intuitively, into havens - where the war is currently losing. Gold is down 6.45% on the month and silver 8.57% in the middle of an active Gulf conflict, and the franc is the weakest currency on this board, because a 5.342% ten-year and a 2.88% real yield outbid fear. That is the single most important thing to understand about this regime: escalation headlines now move oil and European equities far more reliably than they move gold or CHF, so the right way to trade the geopolitics is long USOIL, short GER40 and EU50, and long CAD against the franc and the kiwi - not long bullion. The tail that breaks this framing is a disorderly escalation large enough to make havens trade on fear rather than carry, which would hit XAU and CHF/JPY shorts from both sides at once; the opposite tail is a genuine Hormuz reopening, which collapses the oil premium, relieves the European inflation problem and takes the hawkish tail out of EUR and GBP.
